title: Pies, Pictures and 3D Tricks
objective: After this level you can spot pie charts that don't add to 100% and pictures that exaggerate by growing in two directions at once.
summary: A pie is one whole, so its slices must total 100%. 3D tilts inflate near slices, and Huff's moneybag drawn twice as tall covers four times the area.

cards.headline: A pie chart whose slices add up to more than 100% isn't a pie. It's a warning.
cards.body: Pie charts, picture charts and shiny 3D graphics look friendly. Each has its own way of making some numbers look bigger than they are.

cards.headline: A pie is one whole
cards.body: A pie chart's circle stands for the whole: 100%. So its slices have to add up to 100%. A common way to break that rule is a survey where people could pick more than one answer, like favorite pizza toppings. Those answers can total well over 100%, so they don't belong in a pie. And tilting a pie into 3D makes the slices nearest you look bigger than they are.

cards.headline: Twice as tall, four times as big
cards.body: Picture charts have their own trap, and Huff caught it in 1954. To show a wage of $60 against $30, draw one moneybag twice as tall as the other. Fair? But it's also twice as wide, so it covers four times the area. Read as a solid bag, it looks like eight times the money: $240 instead of $60.

cards.context: The Royal Statistical Society warns that icon charts can mislead because comparing areas is harder than comparing heights. When a chart uses pictures, ask how many times bigger the number is, not how many times bigger the picture looks.

cards.headline: Pies and pictures: checked
learned: Twice as tall means four times the area

questions.prompt: Match each chart with what it really shows or does.

pairs.right: The slices nearest you look bigger

questions.explanation: A pie chart's circle stands for the whole: 100%. Tilting a pie into 3D makes the slices nearest you look bigger, and a moneybag twice as tall is also twice as wide, so it covers four times the area.

questions.prompt: A moneybag is drawn twice as tall to show twice the money. How does that make the difference look bigger?

options.label: The taller bag is drawn in a brighter color
options.rationale: Huff's point was about size, not color.

options.label: It is placed higher up the page
options.rationale: Position is not the trick here.

options.label: The numbers are printed smaller
options.rationale: The numbers are fine; the picture misleads.

options.label: It's also twice as wide, so it covers four times the area

questions.explanation: Twice as tall is also twice as wide: four times the area, and as a solid, eight times the volume.

questions.prompt: Using Level 2's meaning of percent, why can't a pie's slices honestly total 130%?

options.label: Percents above 100 are impossible anywhere
options.rationale: Some percents can exceed 100, like a price rise; a pie cannot.

options.label: A pie can only have four slices
options.rationale: The number of slices is not the issue.

options.label: The whole pie is 100 out of every 100, so nothing is left over
Slices are measured in degrees, not percent
options.rationale: Pies are labelled in percent of the whole.

questions.explanation: A percent counts out of every 100, and the pie is the whole. All the slices together can only be 100 out of 100.
